title: Metrics for Efficacy in FIRST Robotics Programs: Aligning ABET Engineering Student Outcomes with K-12 STEM Educational Practices
extended_summary:
This paper examines how FIRST robotics programs can be evaluated using metrics that align K-12 STEM learning with ABET engineering student outcomes. The authors argue that existing K-12 robotics assessments do not sufficiently connect program outcomes to postsecondary engineering expectations, making it difficult to understand long-term educational value.

The study draws on seven years of Arizona FIRST program evaluation data (2007–2013) from FLL, FTC, and FRC participants, along with coaches, mentors, and parents. The evaluation used mixed methods, including surveys, pre/post STEM BAS instruments, interviews, focus groups, observations, and qualitative coding. The paper maps findings to ABET outcomes such as problem solving, teamwork, communication, lifelong learning, ethical/global awareness, and use of engineering tools.

The main conclusion is that FIRST participation is associated with positive changes in STEM interest, problem-solving, teamwork, communication, planning, and awareness of global issues, while also benefiting coaches and mentors. The authors conclude that FIRST robotics can help prepare K-12 students for success in engineering pathways and that ABET-aligned assessment provides a useful framework for judging program impact.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods program evaluation with survey data, focus groups, and pre-post comparisons, but it is not a controlled causal design and relies heavily on self-report and descriptive statistics. The paper is informative and empirically grounded, but methodological rigor is limited for causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements are generally positive and sometimes statistically significant, but effect sizes are not reported and the outcomes are mostly perception-based rather than direct achievement measures. The likely impact is modest and somewhat unclear for general K-12 populations.

interventions.use_case: FIRST robotics programs (FLL/FTC/FRC) as a hands-on robotics challenge and team-based engineering simulation for K-12 students

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that participation in FIRST robotics was associated with improved STEM interest, basic science understanding, and engineering problem solving. Among FRC participants (n=1423), pre-post STEM BAS scores improved on problem-solving items such as 'I am good at thinking about different solutions' (3.72 to 4.15, p=.001) and 'I like to plan what has to be done ahead of time' (3.85 to 4.00, p=.000), while coach ratings also indicated increased understanding of science principles and use of engineering tools.
finding.measure: STEM BAS pre-post survey items; coach/mentor survey ratings of science and engineering skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds positive changes in students' interest in STEM, school engagement, and motivation to pursue more challenging courses. Coaches and participants reported increased interest in science/technology careers and greater engagement in school, with nationally cited FIRST impact data also noting that 84% of FTC and 90% of FRC participants planned to take more challenging math or science courses.
finding.measure: Coach surveys, participant surveys, and cited FIRST impact-report indicators of school engagement and course intentions

finding.finding_summary: The strongest evidence concerns durable skills such as teamwork, communication, planning, leadership, and problem solving. Across 1,423 participants, coach and student survey results showed gains in teamwork (mean 3.50/4), leadership (3.50/4), presentation skills (3.42/4), and planning skills (3.17/4), with several pre-post STEM BAS items showing statistically significant improvement (e.g., planning and problem-solving items with p<.05).
finding.measure: Coach/mentor survey ratings; student survey items on teamwork, presentation, planning, and problem solving; STEM BAS pre-post comparisons

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in research, writing, and presentation-related communication skills as part of FIRST participation. Student ratings showed improved presentation skills (mean 3.42/4), research skills (3.17/4), and writing skills (2.67/4), indicating that the program supported literacy-adjacent academic practices even though writing was less enjoyed than other activities.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of writing, research, and presentation skills
